causes.text: General Motors recalled nearly 69,000 Chevrolet Bolt electric vehicles worldwide in November 2020 after five battery-related fires. Investigators traced the fires to manufacturing defects in battery cells produced at LG Chem's plant in Ochang, South Korea, prompting the automaker to replace or repair affected battery modules.

source_info.title: GM recalls Chevrolet Bolt EVs over battery fire risk

effects.text: On February 24 2021 Hyundai announced it would replace battery systems in about 82,000 electric vehicles worldwide-including Kona, Ioniq and Elec City models-after a series of fires linked to LG-made cells. The recall, estimated to cost US$900 million, triggered a 3.9% drop in Hyundai's share price and also dragged down shares of its battery supplier LG Chem.

source_info.title: Hyundai to replace EV batteries amid fire risks, shares slide

causal_reasoning_chain.description: In November 2020 General Motors recalled nearly 69,000 Chevrolet Bolt EVs worldwide after investigators linked five battery fires to defective cells produced by LG Chem. The recall underscored systemic risks associated with battery manufacturing and drew global attention to the safety of LG-supplied cells.

The GM recall raised regulatory and consumer scrutiny of other automakers that used similar LG battery chemistry. Concerns about latent defects and potential fires created pressure for proactive safety checks and heightened the reputational stakes for companies using the same supplier.

After several fires in its own Kona EVs, Hyundai announced on 24 February 2021 that it would replace the battery systems of 82,000 vehicles worldwide, including those using LG cells. The costly recall wiped nearly 4 percent off Hyundai's share price as investors reacted to the financial and reputational damage.

rationale: GM's high-profile battery recall highlighted safety problems in LG-supplied cells and triggered scrutiny across the EV industry. Hyundai's subsequent decision to replace batteries in its own EVs stemmed from the same defect, and the market's negative reaction underscores the direct cost and reputational hit associated with large recalls.
counterfactual_analysis: If GM had not recalled its Bolt EVs due to LG battery fires, regulators and consumers might have been less attuned to potential defects in similar cells. Without that early warning, Hyundai could have delayed its own recall, potentially avoiding the immediate share-price drop but risking larger losses if additional fires occurred later.

adversarial_confounders.text: Global semiconductor shortages in early 2021 limited automotive production.
adversarial_confounders.impact: Supply-chain disruptions could also have contributed to investor pessimism about Hyundai's earnings potential.

details.commentary: Automakers rely on a small group of advanced battery suppliers, so a quality failure at one vendor can quickly cascade across customers. When GM's Bolt recall exposed problems at LG's cells, Hyundai had limited room to negotiate or switch suppliers and had to absorb the fallout.

details.pestel_factor: Legal - product safety regulation and recall standards
details.commentary: High-profile EV fires triggered tougher safety expectations from regulators and the public. Under this legal pressure, Hyundai moved to replace suspect packs to satisfy authorities and reassure drivers.

Each new fire and recall story heightened concern and made a broader battery replacement program more likely. The sequence of incidents, scrutiny and defensive recalls created a reinforcing loop linking LG-related problems to Hyundai's final decision.
